sentences: Huge boulders are piled one upon another, as if they were blocking the mouth of a valley.
Beneath them a scholar rides past on a donkey, followed by a servant on foot.
This is the Entrance to Yeongtong Valley, one leaf from the Album of a Journey to Songdo, painted by the scholar-artist Kang Se-hwang, who used the pen name Pyoam.
Songdo is the old name of Kaesong, the former capital of the Goryeo kingdom.
Around 1757, Kang toured its famous sights and recorded the journey in a single album of pictures and writing.
That album now belongs to the National Museum of Korea in Seoul.
Kang was a scholar gifted in poetry, calligraphy and painting alike.
He was also famous as a critic whose comments on other artists' work were eagerly sought, and he came to be seen as the elder statesman of the art world of his day.
As a boy, the great painter Kim Hong-do studied with him.
Now look closely at the rocks.
Each boulder is as big as a house.
Yet they are not drawn in the usual way, with brushstrokes that trace the cracks and texture of the stone.
Instead, Kang washed on pale ink and blue-green colour, so that each rounded mass has a lit side and a side in shade.
Because of this, the rocks do not lie flat on the paper; they swell out as solid, heavy forms.
Scholars see the influence of Western painting in this handling of light and shade.
At the time, Western pictures and books were trickling into Joseon by way of Beijing, and curious scholars like Kang studied them with great interest.
Look at the rider below the rocks.
He is painted very small, and his tiny size tells you at once how enormous the boulders really are.
Many viewers like to imagine him as the painter himself, pausing for a moment on his journey to stare up at them.
Other leaves in the album were just as new.
In the view of the streets of Kaesong, the road narrows and the houses shrink as they recede into the distance.
Kang was working out near and far the way the eye actually sees them, rather than following the old formulas.
In the empty space above the boulders, Kang wrote a passage in his own hand.
Picture and words belong together here, as they do in so much Korean scholar painting, where the brush that paints is also the brush that writes.
If Jeong Seon had opened the way to painting Korea's own landscape through Korean eyes, Kang added a new way of seeing on top of it.
He laid an unfamiliar technique carefully over a living tradition, and made it entirely his own.
Step back and take in the whole leaf: giant rocks and a tiny person, side by side.
The surprise of a traveller meeting this place for the first time still reaches us, nearly two hundred and seventy years later.
Where would your own journey stop, just to look?
